analysis.one_liner: Designates 1.5 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain as wilderness, permanently barring oil drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 29 senators from both parties, was referred to committee the day it was introduced and died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska — the coastal plain known as the "1002 Area" — to the National Wilderness Preservation System [S2] [S3]. Once land is designated wilderness, federal law bars roads, motorized vehicles, and commercial development, including oil and gas leasing. The practical effect would have been to permanently close the most hotly contested potential drilling site in the country to oil exploration. The bill was introduced on April 22, 1999, read twice, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it never received a hearing or vote [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the general public would have gained permanent protection of a unique Arctic ecosystem — calving grounds for the Porcupine caribou herd, habitat for polar bears and migratory birds, and a wild landscape open only to people on foot. Future generations would keep the choice of a wilderness intact rather than an oil field, and the refuge's subsistence users, including Gwich'in communities who depend on the caribou herd, would keep their way of life secure.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic refuge — the coastal plain depicted on the 1991 'Alternative E' wilderness map — to the National Wilderness Preservation System under the Wilderness Act [S3].

The designation applies to the same 1002 Area that federal studies have long identified as the refuge's only zone with significant oil potential, meaning the bill's conservation effect is concentrated exactly where drilling advocates have sought access.
Because wilderness designation is permanent under the Wilderness Act, the protection could not be reversed by a future administration or a later Congress without new legislation.

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry would lose access to the coastal plain, one of the largest unexplored onshore potential oil areas in the United States. Alaska's state government would forgo potential royalties and revenue from development, and consumers could see marginally higher energy prices or greater reliance on imports compared with a drilling scenario. Supporters of drilling also argue the region could have produced federal revenue and jobs.

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently lock away a substantial potential domestic oil supply. The coastal plain has been estimated by federal assessments to hold billions of barrels of technically recoverable oil, and closing it forecloses that supply, the federal revenue it would generate, and any offset to oil imports [S3].

Wilderness designation is irreversible in practice: unlike a management decision, it cannot be adjusted as energy conditions change, which is the strongest good-faith objection from drilling supporters and many Alaska officials.

Some Alaska Native residents of the coastal plain area, such as the community of Kaktovik, have historically supported development as a source of jobs and local revenue, and permanent wilderness designation would foreclose that option for them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tradeoff is stark and one-time: permanent, irrevocable protection of the last large intact Arctic coastal ecosystem in the United States, against forgoing an uncertain but potentially large oil reserve and the revenue and jobs it might have produced. How one weighs it depends largely on how much weight you give permanent conservation versus domestic energy supply. The bill itself was cleanly drafted — it simply extended an existing wilderness designation to the remaining core of the refuge — so the dispute was over the policy choice, not the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. William Roth introduced the bill on April 22, 1999, joined by 22 original cosponsors including both Republicans and Democrats [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where it remained for the rest of the Congress [S5].
Cosponsorship grew to 28 senators — 24 Democrats and 4 Republicans — but the committee took no action and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S4] [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests and drilling advocates were better off, because the coastal plain stayed legally available for development efforts in later Congresses — including the ultimately successful push to open it to leasing in 2017. Supporters of wilderness protection gained nothing except the record of bipartisan support the bill amassed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies seeking refuge drilling access

for.name: Sen. William V. Roth Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Delaware, lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Earth Day 1999 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 24 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the wilderness designation, including Sens. Baucus, Lieberman, Boxer, Kennedy, and Feinstein.

for.name: 4 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Environment and Public Works Chairman John Chafee of Rhode Island and Jim Jeffords of Vermont.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 22, 1999, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Alaska's senators, Frank Murkowski and Ted Stevens
against.what_they_did: Led the long-running push to open the Arctic refuge coastal plain to oil drilling and opposed wilderness designation, using their seniority to champion development.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Developers seeking access to the coastal plain
against.what_they_did: Funded a sustained lobbying campaign across the 1990s and 2000s to open the 1002 Area to leasing, framing the bill's protections as a lockout of domestic energy supply.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 24 of 45 Senate Democrats signed on versus 4 of 55 Senate Republicans — though a bipartisan handful of Republicans, including the committee chairman, backed it.

industries.note: Wilderness designation would permanently close the refuge coastal plain — the country's most sought-after unexplored onshore oil prospect — to leasing and development. The industry's gain from the bill's death is the public's loss of the option to keep the plain un-drilled, since the land stayed open to future drilling attempts.

The state forgoes potential royalties, taxes, and jobs from coastal plain development if the area is locked up as wilderness. Its interest in development ran against the conservation outcome most of the bill's supporters sought.
